cf.title: Improve row estimation with multi-column unique indexes

input.subject: Improve row estimation with multi-column unique indexes

verdict_reasoning: The goal is accepted by the only reviewer, and no objection survived at level 1. Two level 2 objections survived. standards-compat-1: v3 gives an index path rows=1 while the relation estimate stays high, and message #3 does not answer the README rule raised in message #2. standards-compat-3: v2 and v3 disagree on deferrable unique constraints. The thread needs to settle both before code review.

brief.title: Clamp row estimates to one for full-key matches on multi-column unique indexes
brief.problem: When equality clauses cover all key columns of a multi-column unique index, the planner multiplies per-column selectivities and can estimate many rows (2149 in the example). The inflated cost can make the planner pick another index, such as one matching ORDER BY, over the unique lookup. This affects any query that looks up rows by a composite unique key.
brief.proposed_design: v3 adds a "unique path" flag on IndexPath, set by a new is_path_unique when index paths are built: a unique index with at least one equality clause on every key column. cost_index then sets the path rows to 1, genericcostestimate sets selectivity to 1.0/reltuples, and btcostestimate uses the flag for numIndexTuples = 1. v2 (Chengpeng Yan) instead clamps the relation-level estimate in set_baserel_size_estimates() and get_parameterized_baserel_size().
user_visible_surface: Changed planner row estimates and plan choice for equality lookups on all key columns of a multi-column unique index.
C API: new unique_path field in IndexPath, visible to extensions that build or inspect index paths.
Equality lookups on the full key of a multi-column unique index are treated as returning at most one row, with no new SQL syntax, GUC or catalog column.
author_claims: In the example the estimate drops from 2149 rows to 1, and the planner keeps the unique index instead of switching to an index on id.
A relation-level clamp, as in v2, does not work for unique partial indexes, so the one-row bound belongs to the path.
IS NULL counts as equality when the index uses NULLS NOT DISTINCT.
For deferrable unique constraints, a one-row estimate is usually closer to the truth than a statistics-based estimate.
When the path is unique, most selectivity work can be skipped (0003).
brief.thread_state: Chengpeng Yan agreed the problem is real but said v1 lowered rows at the wrong level and posted v2 with a relation-level clamp. The author answered with v3, a path-level design, and nobody has replied to v3 since July.
unclear: v3 gives different row counts to paths of the same relation and parameterization, which v2 says the optimizer README expects to be equal; the author does not address this.
The thread has no decision on deferrable unique constraints: v2 excludes them and the author asks whether the current behaviour is deliberate.
No one says how the one-row path estimate interacts with join size estimates that use the relation-level row count.
The thread does not say whether index AMs other than B-tree get the unique path behaviour.
There is no planning-time or regression benchmark beyond the single example.

prior_attempts.title: Revert "Use Foreign Key relationships to infer multi-column join selectivity".
prior_attempts.quote: We found multiple bugs in this feature, and there was concern about possible planner slowdown (though to be fair, exhibiting a very large slowdown proved difficult).
prior_attempts.reason:
This commit reverts 137805f89 as well as the associated commits 015e88942,
5306df283, and 68d704edb.  We found multiple bugs in this feature, and
there was concern about possible planner slowdown (though to be fair,
exhibiting a very large slowdown proved difficult).  The way forward
requires a considerable rewrite, which may or may not be possible to
accomplish in time for beta2.  In my judgment reviewing the rewrite will
be easier to accomplish starting from a clean slate, so let's temporarily
revert what's there now.  This also leaves us in a safe state if it turns
out to be necessary to postpone the rewrite to the next development cycle.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P24 used foreign keys to infer join selectivity across relations. This proposal uses unique indexes to bound one relation's scan to one row, with a much smaller scope.

objections.title: Paths of one relation get different row counts for the same clauses
objections.failure_scenario: A query joins visitor on (org, name). The index scan path reports rows=1, while the seq scan, bitmap path and the join size, which use the relation estimate, still report about 2149. EXPLAIN shows a scan with rows=1 under a join sized from 2149, and the user cannot tell which estimate the planner acted on.
objections.argument: Message #2 says the optimizer README expects paths for the same relation and parameterization to share one row count. v3 keeps the path-level design and sets rows only on the IndexPath. Message #3 answers with partial unique indexes but says nothing about the README rule or about join estimates. A committer would likely want a relation-level clamp where it is valid, plus a path-level clamp only for partial indexes, with a stated reason for that exception.
objections.author_must_show: For which index types and plan shapes may index paths report fewer rows than the relation, and how do join size estimates stay consistent with that?

critic.reasoning: The optimizer README requires equal row counts for paths of one relation and parameterization, and join size estimates use the relation-level row count. Message #3 answers only the partial-index point, so the inconsistency is unanswered.

objections.title: Deferrable unique constraints changed without a decision in the thread
objections.failure_scenario: A transaction loads rows under a deferred unique constraint and then joins against the table on the full key before commit. The planner assumes one row per key and picks a nested loop. Duplicates exist until commit, so the join runs much slower than planned, and nothing in EXPLAIN explains why.
objections.argument: v2 excludes deferrable constraints. Message #3 keeps them and argues that one row is usually closer to the truth. That argument is reasonable, but it extends the B-tree shortcut to multi-column keys without a recorded decision. A committer would likely want the choice made explicitly and documented, because this is the case where the estimate can be wrong by the size of the batch.
objections.author_must_show: Should deferrable unique constraints count toward the one-row bound, and what behaviour do bulk loads inside the deferral window get?

critic.reasoning: The existing btcostestimate shortcut also ignores deferrability, but it only sets numIndexTuples. v3 extends the assumption to path rows, which affects join choice, and v2 and v3 disagree on this with no decision in the thread.

refuted.title: New IndexPath field reuses the existing UniquePath name
refuted.failure_scenario: An extension author or a later patch reads IndexPath->unique_path and confuses it with UniquePath, the existing path node for unique-ification. They may also treat it as a uniqueness proof for join removal or inner_unique. With deferrable constraints, that proof would be wrong.
refuted.argument: pathnodes.h already uses "unique path" for UniquePath, so the name is taken. v3 also counts deferrable constraints as unique (message #3), but relation_has_unique_index_for() requires immediate uniqueness for proofs. A field named like a proof that holds only for costing invites misuse in later patches, and nothing fails loudly when that happens.
refuted.author_must_show: Can the field get a name that does not collide with UniquePath and that says it only bounds the estimate, not uniqueness?

critic.reasoning: The scenario depends on a hypothetical later patch misreading the field as a uniqueness proof. The field name is a code-level naming point, which is outside levels 1-2; the deferrable question is covered by standards-compat-3.

refuted.title: Path-level row clamp breaks equal rowcounts across paths of one relation
refuted.failure_scenario: A unique-path index scan reports rows=1 while the seq scan and other index paths of the same relation report 2149, and join sizing uses rel->rows = 2149. Later patches that assume path rows equal rel rows, such as path comparison or join costing, produce mismatched plans. Nothing fails loudly, so the mismatch surfaces as plan-regression reports in the field.
refuted.argument: Message #2 states that the optimizer README expects paths for the same relation and parameterization to have equal rowcounts, and v3 departs from that. Message #3 answers only that a relation-level clamp misses unique partial indexes, and does not say why breaking the invariant is safe or what else relies on it. The invariant becomes a special case that future planner work must remember. A committer would likely ask for the invariant to be kept, or for its exception to be documented and justified.
refuted.author_must_show: Which planner code relies on equal path rowcounts per relation, and why does a rows=1 IndexPath alongside a larger rel->rows not mislead it?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1, which states the same README rule with a more concrete scenario.

refuted.title: Planner flag on IndexPath sidesteps the amcostestimate interface
refuted.failure_scenario: An extension index AM that supports unique indexes ignores the new IndexPath field and keeps computing selectivity from per-column statistics. cost_index still forces path rows to 1, so its cost and its rowcount disagree. The extension author learns of this only from plan anomalies, since no interface change forces an update.
refuted.argument: Message #3 places the flag in IndexPath and says passing it to amcostestimate would require changing that interface, so v3 avoids the change. As a result, uniqueness knowledge is split between generic planner code (cost_index, genericcostestimate) and B-tree-specific code (btcostestimate), and other AMs get the behaviour only if they inspect the path. The proposal does not say which AMs are covered.
refuted.author_must_show: How does an index AM other than B-tree learn about and consistently honour the unique path, and why is an implicit IndexPath field better than an explicit amcostestimate argument?

critic.reasoning: amcostestimate already receives the IndexPath, so the flag reaches every AM through the existing interface, and AMs that call genericcostestimate get the selectivity change. B-tree is the only in-core AM with unique indexes, and the objection names no affected extension AM.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: v3 adds a unique_path field to IndexPath in pathnodes.h and touches pathnode.h, which extensions that build index paths see.

touch_points.label: planner behaviour change
touch_points.reason: Row estimates and plan choice change for full-key equality lookups on multi-column unique indexes.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: A path-level row count that differs from the relation estimate is an exception later planner work must keep in mind.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: is_path_unique runs each time index paths are built, and the thread shows no planning-time measurement.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: How do join size estimates, which use the relation-level row count, stay consistent with an index path that reports rows=1?
Why not clamp at relation level where relation_has_unique_index_for() applies, and keep a path-level clamp only for unique partial indexes?
Should deferrable unique constraints count toward the one-row bound, given that v2 excludes them and duplicates can exist until commit?
Do index AMs other than B-tree get the unique path behaviour, and through which code path?
What is the planning-time cost of is_path_unique on queries with many indexes, and do any existing regression plans change?

committability.owner_note: Someone who knows planner size estimation and index costing (costsize.c, selfuncs.c, indxpath.c). No such committer has posted in the three-message thread.
committability.liability: Plan regressions from changed estimates on a common query pattern, in every later release. The owner also has to defend any exception to the equal-row-count rule for paths of one relation.
committability.author_follow_up: The author answered the review within three days with a reworked v3 and has moved the entry across three CommitFests.

priority.reason: Lookups by a composite unique key are common, and the reviewer in message #2 agrees the misestimate is real. v2 and v3 differ on the level of the clamp and on deferrable constraints, and the patch touches core planner costing files.

provisional_note: The code was not read. Not judged: whether is_path_unique handles IS NULL, arrays and partial-index predicates correctly, and which callers read the path row count that v3 changes.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Remove useless GROUP BY columns considering unique index
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets remove_useless_groupby_columns use unique constraints whose columns are all NOT NULL, in addition to the primary key, to drop functionally dependent GROUP BY columns. When several candidates exist, it picks the one with the fewest columns so that the most columns can be removed.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch no longer applied because it relied on catalogued NOT NULL constraints, which had been removed. David Rowley also objected to choosing the constraint with the fewest columns, which ignores column width and can pick a constraint with no columns in the GROUP BY clause, a regression against today's primary-key behaviour. The author said he would study the advice and update, but the visible messages show no new version before the entry was returned.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
It looks like it  won't work if the UNIQUE constraint with
the least columns gets no mention in the GROUP BY clause. That'll
cause performance regressions from what we have today when the primary
key is mentioned and columns can be removed using that but a UNIQUE
constraint exists which has no corresponding GROUP BY columns and
fewer unique columns than the PK.

precedents_retrieved.title: NOT VALID for Unique Indexes
precedents_retrieved.summary: Simon Riggs proposed allowing an existing index to be switched between unique and non-unique via ALTER INDEX SET [NOT] UNIQUE [NOT VALID] and ALTER INDEX VALIDATE UNIQUE, so uniqueness could be added without a long write-excluding scan and validated later in a separate transaction. The WIP patch added a new pg_index column (induniquevalid) and did not yet implement the index validation scan.
precedents_retrieved.objection: No deciding objection was raised; reviewers were positive and asked only design questions. The author said he could not finish the patch for the next commitfest and would complete it later, and a later message noted the patch no longer applied to HEAD and asked for an updated version, with no reply shown. The entry was left incomplete with no updated version posted.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I won't be able to finish this patch in time for this next CF, but
thanks for your interest, I will complete for PG15 later this year.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Optimize order of GROUP BY keys".
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Optimize order of GROUP BY keys".
Reverted commit(s): Optimize order of GROUP BY keys
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit db0d67db2401eb6238ccc04c6407a4fd4f985832 and
several follow-on fixes.  The idea of making a cost-based choice
of the order of the sorting columns is not fundamentally unsound,
but it requires cost information and data statistics that we don't
really have.  For example, relying on procost to distinguish the
relative costs of different sort comparators is pretty pointless
so long as most such comparator functions are labeled with cost 1.0.
Moreover, estimating the number of comparisons done by Quicksort
requires more than just an estimate of the number of distinct values
in the input: you also need some idea of the sizes of the larger
groups, if you want an estimate that's good to better than a factor of
three or so.  That's data that's often unknown or not very reliable.
Worse, to arrive at estimates of the number of calls made to the
lower-order-column comparison functions, the code needs to make
estimates of the numbers of distinct values of multiple columns,
which are necessarily even less trustworthy than per-column stats.
Even if all the inputs are perfectly reliable, the cost algorithm
as-implemented cannot offer useful information about how to order
sorting columns beyond the point at which the average group size
is estimated to drop to 1.

Close inspection of the code added by db0d67db2 shows that there
are also multiple small bugs.  These could have been fixed, but
there's not much point if we don't trust the estimates to be
accurate in-principle.

Finally, the changes in cost_sort's behavior made for very large
changes (often a factor of 2 or so) in the cost estimates for all
sorting operations, not only those for multi-column GROUP BY.
That naturally changes plan choices in many situations, and there's
precious little evidence to show that the changes are for the better.
Given the above doubts about whether the new estimates are really
trustworthy, it's hard to summon much confidence that these changes
are better on the average.

Since we're hard up against the release deadline for v15, let's
revert these changes for now.  We can always try again later.

Note: in v15, I left T_PathKeyInfo in place in nodes.h even though
it's unreferenced.  Removing it would be an ABI break, and it seems
a bit late in the release cycle for that.

precedents_retrieved.title: Improve amcheck to check UNIQUE constraint in btree index
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Peter Geoghegan, Mark Dilger, David Steele
precedents_retrieved.summary: Extend contrib/amcheck's bt_index_check and bt_index_parent_check so that, for btree indexes with a UNIQUE constraint, they detect duplicate keys whose heap tuples are visible, including duplicates spanning adjacent leaf pages, and report the index and heap TIDs involved. Later versions added an optional argument to enable the uniqueness check and a regression test variant for 32-bit systems.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers asked for further changes: Peter Geoghegan objected to reporting violations as WARNINGs, to the message saying an index only might be corrupt (calling it an unacceptable false positive), to the handling of cross-page duplicates, and to tests that update pg_index, and suggested opclass-based fault injection and sharing the heapallindexed snapshot. Mark Dilger's review of v4 asked for documentation updates, pg_amcheck integration with TAP tests, and a different test approach. No updated patch followed for several weeks, and David Steele marked it Returned with Feedback because it needed more work and had not been updated.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This patch appears to need some work and has not been updated in several
weeks, so marking Returned with Feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Allow foreign keys to reference a superset of unique columns
precedents_retrieved.summary: Allow a foreign key constraint to reference a set of columns that is a superset of the columns of a non-deferrable unique or primary key index on the referenced table, rather than requiring an exact match. An optional USING INDEX clause after the referenced column list would name the supporting unique index where the choice would otherwise be ambiguous.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that the semantics are questionable (for example CASCADE behaviour of the extra columns, nullable subset columns, MATCH PARTIAL and UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT), that the change could break existing optimizations, and that it risks conflict with the SQL standard and its information_schema. He said a patch was premature unless the SQL committee standardized the behaviour. Peter Eisentraut said that working out the full specification was the open work still required of the proposal.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I think the semantics are at best questionable, I think
it will break important optimizations, and I think the chances of
finding ourselves in conflict with some future SQL spec extension are
too high.

precedents_retrieved.title: Using multicolumn statistics for more precise join selectivity estimatation
precedents_retrieved.objectors: vignesh C, Yugo NAGATA, Tomas Vondra
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch had two parts. One let the planner use extended (multicolumn) statistics, specifically functional dependencies, when estimating join selectivity. The other made auto_explain create multicolumn statistics automatically, or just suggest them, when a plan node's estimated row count differs from the actual count by more than a threshold.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The last visible message (July 2021) reports that the patch no longer compiled on Windows against changed ModifyTableState fields. The same message says Yugo Nagata's open review comments still needed addressing, and the entry was moved to Waiting on Author. Those comments included duplicate statistics suggestions causing a unique-constraint error, redundant suggestions, and a request to explain why each statistic is suggested. Earlier, Tomas Vondra had suggested moving the advisor into a separate extension rather than auto_explain, collecting data across many runs, and not creating statistics automatically. The visible messages show no new version after that, and the entry was returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Also Yugo Nagata's comments need to be addressed, I'm changing the
status to "Waiting for Author".

precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch fixes a typo in the comment for estimate_multivariate_ndistinct(), changing "If a match it found" to "If a match is found". It changes only the comment, not any code.

precedents_retrieved.title: Inconsistency in owner assignment between INDEX and STATISTICS
precedents_retrieved.summary: The proposal makes CREATE STATISTICS record the table owner as the owner of the statistics object, as CREATE INDEX does, in place of the user who runs the command. The patch sets stxowner from the relation's relowner in CreateStatistics() and keeps the permission check on the current user.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Amit Khandekar pointed out that the documentation states statistics ownership is independent of the underlying table, so the creator owning the object is intended. He also showed that the reproduction was wrong: the statistics object was created in the default schema, and dropping it there gives the expected "must be owner" error. The author agreed with both points and withdrew the proposal.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I think, since there is no permanent association of ownership between
the table and the statistics, it makes sense for the user who is
running the create command to own the statistics, regardless of who
the user is, provided that the user has privileges.

precedents_retrieved.title: Adjust tuples estimate for appendrel
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch sets an appendrel's tuples estimate to the sum of the tuples of its live child relations instead of to its rows estimate. This lets estimate_num_groups() apply the formula from 84f9a35e3 to appendrels, which reduces the over-estimate of distinct groups that made the planner under-cost incremental sort.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. Andrei Lepikhov supported committing the patch but asked for a regression test that checks the appendrel->tuples change directly, and the author had said he could not devise one. After that the discussion moved to wider ndistinct estimation ideas, and no later message from the author is shown.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert applying column aliases to the output of whole-row Vars.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert applying column aliases to the output of whole-row Vars.
Reverted commit(s): Ensure that RowExprs and whole-row Vars produce the expected column names.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
In commit bf7ca1587, I had the bright idea that we could make the
result of a whole-row Var (that is, foo.*) track any column aliases
that had been applied to the FROM entry the Var refers to.  However,
that's not terribly logically consistent, because now the output of
the Var is no longer of the named composite type that the Var claims
to emit.  bf7ca1587 tried to handle that by changing the output
tuple values to be labeled with a blessed RECORD type, but that's
really pretty disastrous: we can wind up storing such tuples onto
disk, whereupon they're not readable by other sessions.

The only practical fix I can see is to give up on what bf7ca1587
tried to do, and say that the column names of tuples produced by
a whole-row Var are always those of the underlying named composite
type, query aliases or no.  While this introduces some inconsistencies,
it removes others, so it's not that awful in the abstract.  What *is*
kind of awful is to make such a behavioral change in a back-patched
bug fix.  But corrupt data is worse, so back-patched it will be.

(A workaround available to anyone who's unhappy about this is to
introduce an extra level of sub-SELECT, so that the whole-row Var is
referring to the sub-SELECT's output and not to a named table type.
Then the Var is of type RECORD to begin with and there's no issue.)

Per report from Miles Delahunty.  The faulty commit dates to 9.5,
so back-patch to all supported branches.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Use Foreign Key relationships to infer multi-column join selectivity".
precedents_retrieved.authors: Simon Riggs, Tom Lane, Robert Haas
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Use Foreign Key relationships to infer multi-column join selectivity".
Reverted commit(s): Use Foreign Key relationships to infer multi-column join selectivity; Load FK defs into relcache for use by planner; Clean up foreign-key caching code in planner.; Minimal fix for crash bug in quals_match_foreign_key.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This commit reverts 137805f89 as well as the associated commits 015e88942,
5306df283, and 68d704edb.  We found multiple bugs in this feature, and
there was concern about possible planner slowdown (though to be fair,
exhibiting a very large slowdown proved difficult).  The way forward
requires a considerable rewrite, which may or may not be possible to
accomplish in time for beta2.  In my judgment reviewing the rewrite will
be easier to accomplish starting from a clean slate, so let's temporarily
revert what's there now.  This also leaves us in a safe state if it turns
out to be necessary to postpone the rewrite to the next development cycle.

roaster_notes.note: No listed precedent is the same idea. P24's revert reason, bugs and possible planner slowdown, is generic and would apply to any planner change, so it does not support an objection here. The thread cites no earlier discussion of this idea.
The proposal adds no syntax, GUC, catalog object or pg_dump state, so those touch points do not apply.

The proposal changes only planner estimates and costing, with no on-disk, WAL, catalog, replication or wire protocol change. The new IndexPath field, and any create_index_path signature change in pathnode.h, is normal churn for a major version and the patch is not proposed for backpatching.

The proposal changes only planner row estimates and costs for full-key equality lookups on unique indexes, and it adds no new privilege, object, function or exposed data. A wrong one-row estimate, for example from a deferrable constraint, affects plan quality only on the table owner's own data, so it is not a privilege or exposure issue.
The fit with core is sound: composite unique-key lookups are a general case. No committer has engaged across three CommitFests, which affects committability only and is not counted as an objection.

No existing Postgres feature or extension gives a one-row estimate for full-key equality on a multi-column unique index. Extended statistics do not reliably produce that bound, and a planner hint extension only forces a plan without fixing the estimate. v3's is_path_unique extracts and generalizes the existing btcostestimate check, so it does not add a second mechanism. Whether it should sit beside relation_has_unique_index_for is a design question for another angle.

Demand holds up from this angle: lookups by a composite unique key are a common query pattern, and the only reviewer (message #2) agreed the misestimate is a real planner problem. The evidence is one synthetic skewed example with no field report, but the cost falls mainly on queries that match a full unique key, so a demand objection would not stand.
